title: brulee_tab_icl() errors with 'subscript out of bounds' when training_set_limit drops a near-constant column
description:
## Summary

`brulee_tab_icl()` / `tabular_icl()` can throw `Error: subscript out of bounds` at predict time when `training_set_limit` subsamples the training context small enough that a rare near-binary categorical column becomes constant in the subsample.

## Root cause

In `R/tabicl-ensemble.R`, `tabicl_classifier_proba()` and `tabicl_regressor_stats()` call `tabicl_unique_filter()` on the *stored, subsampled* training context (`object$train_x`, i.e. after `training_set_limit` has already dropped rows), filtering out any column with a single unique value:

```r
keep <- tabicl_unique_filter(x_train)
xtr <- x_train[, keep, drop = FALSE]
xte <- x_test[, keep, drop = FALSE]
```

But in `R/tabicl-predict.R`, the ensemble's per-member feature-permutation indices are built from the *unfiltered* column count, before that filtering happens:

```r
members <- tabicl_make_members(
  object$num_estimators,
  ncol(object$train_x),   # unfiltered column count
  ...
)
```

When a column is dropped by `tabicl_unique_filter()` (because the subsampled context happens to have no variation left in that column), `member$feat`'s indices can exceed the number of columns actually present in `cached$tr`/`cached$te`, and

```r
x_cat <- rbind(cached$tr, cached$te)[, member$feat, drop = FALSE]
```

in `tabicl_member_input()` (`R/tabicl-ensemble.R`) fails with `subscript out of bounds`.

This is most likely to happen with `training_set_limit` set well below the full training set size, on data with a rare binary/near-constant categorical predictor (e.g. an indicator that's `1` in only a handful of rows).

## Reproducible example

```r
library(tabby)
library(brulee)

set.seed(321)
n <- 300
synthetic <- data.frame(
  y    = rnorm(n, 100, 10),
  x1   = rnorm(n),
  x2   = rnorm(n),
  rare = factor(c(1, rep(0, n - 1)))  # one positive row out of 300
)

spec <- tabular_icl(mode = "regression") |>
  set_engine("brulee", training_set_limit = 50)
wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe(y ~ ., data = synthetic)) |>
  add_model(spec)

set.seed(1)
fit_obj <- fit(wf, data = synthetic)
predict(fit_obj, new_data = synthetic[1:5, ])
#> Error in `rbind(cached$tr, cached$te)[, member$feat, drop = FALSE]`:
#> ! subscript out of bounds
```

Reproduces on every seed tried (1–8) with this `rare` column, because `training_set_limit = 50` out of 300 rows has a high chance of excluding the single `rare = 1` row, making that column constant in the subsampled context.

Also reproduced on a real-world regression dataset (~680 training rows, `training_set_limit` below ~250) where a `waterfront` indicator is `1` in only 4 of 682 rows.

## Suggested fix

Compute `tabicl_make_members()`'s `n_features` argument from the *filtered* (post-`tabicl_unique_filter()`) column count rather than `ncol(object$train_x)`, or apply the same unique-value filter once at fit time (on the stored/subsampled context) so the filtered column count is stable and known before member feature-permutations are generated.

## Session info

```
brulee 1.2.0
tabby 0.0.1
torch 0.17.0
R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24)
```

title: TabPFN slowness
description:
Related to #143 


I've noticed that the TabPFN implementation here is a little slow. On `mtcars`, fitting `brulee_tab_pfn()` and calling `augment()` once takes about 10.8 s on the CPU. The same steps with `brulee_tab_icl()` take 4.4 s.

```r
library(brulee)

system.time({
  set.seed(1)
  pfn_fit <- brulee_tab_pfn(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars[3:32, ])
  pfn_pred <- augment(pfn_fit, mtcars[1:2, ], quantile_levels = (1:4) / 5)
})
#>    user  system elapsed
#>  16.821   0.953  10.779
```

### Where the time goes

These timings come from a fresh R session on the CPU, using v3.5 with the default 8 ensemble members:

| Step | Time |
| --- | --- |
| sha256 of the 876 MB v3.5 checkpoint (first fit of each R session) | 3.7 s |
| Read the checkpoint, build the model, load the weights | 1.5 s |
| A later fit in the same session | 0.07 s |
| `predict()` or `augment()` | 4.7 s |
| The same prediction without the between-layer garbage collection | 0.4 s |

Two costs dominate. Neither is the model's computation.

1. **Garbage collection between layers (about 4.3 s of each prediction).**
   - R torch frees tensor memory only when R's garbage collector runs. To stop memory from piling up on large data, `tabpfn_release()` calls `gc(full = TRUE)` after each layer and attention chunk.
   - One prediction makes 57 of these calls. Each takes about 0.075 s, because a full collection walks the whole R heap.
   - On small data that is about 90% of the prediction time, and it saves no memory worth having.
   - The collections are needed for large data: without them, the `forested` example runs out of memory on MPS.
2. **Checksum verification in every session (3.7 s on the first fit).**
   - Before the first use in an R session, the whole checkpoint is hashed to confirm it is complete and is the expected release.
   - The result is only kept for the session, so every new session pays the cost again.
   - TabICL's weights are about a quarter of the size and aren't hashed.

The rest is expected work. The v3.5 checkpoint is about four times the size of TabICL's (1.5 s to read and build), and the default ensemble has 8 members.

MPS was faster in the original timings (8.6 s), largely because GPU memory is freed differently, so the forced collections cost less there.

### Proposed fixes

- **Collect garbage only when it pays.**
  - `tabpfn_forward()` knows the size of each forward pass, so it can turn the between-layer collections on only above a size threshold. The threshold would be a new option, `brulee.tabpfn_release_cells`, with a default set by measuring peak memory at several data sizes.
  - Also measure whether a minor collection, `gc(full = FALSE)`, frees enough memory at a fraction of the cost.
  - Large data keeps the current protection.
- **Remember verified checkpoints across sessions.**
  - After a successful check, store the file's path, size, modification time, and sha256 in brulee's TabPFN cache. Later sessions skip the hash while all of these match.
  - Any change to the file forces a full check again.
  - `tab_pfn_clear_cache()` removes the records.

Predictions should not change. The goal is about 2 s for fit plus `augment()` in the first session and under 1 s in later ones. The existing parity tests check that predictions are unchanged, and the `forested` example on CPU and MPS checks large data still fits in memory.

title: predict() does not clamp an out-of-range epoch, and its bounds check is off by one
description:
`predict()` errors instead of clamping when `epoch` is past the end of the fit, and its bounds check is off by one. `coef()` already handles this correctly, so the fix is to make `predict()` match it.

## Two defects

**1. `last_epoch_note()` warns but never clamps.** It says "so last epoch is used" and then returns `invisible(NULL)` (`R/0_utils.R:417-426`). Every caller discards the return value and goes on to index `model$estimates[[epoch + 1]]`, which errors. The warning promises a fallback that does not happen:

- `R/mlp-predict.R:92`
- `R/linear_reg-predict.R:82`
- `R/logistic_reg-predict.R:90`
- `R/multinomial_reg-predict.R:86`
- `R/resnet-predict.R:94`
- `R/autoint-predict.R:80`
- `R/saint-predict.R:79`

**2. The bounds check is off by one.** The bridges set `max_epoch <- length(model$estimates)` and test `if (epoch > max_epoch)`. Because `estimates` includes epoch zero as its first element and indexing is `estimates[[epoch + 1]]`, the largest valid epoch is `length(estimates) - 1`. So `epoch == length(estimates)` passes the guard, emits **no warning at all**, and then errors.

`brulee_rln()` is not exempt: `R/rln-predict.R:78-82` does clamp, but to `max_epoch`, i.e. `length(estimates)`, so it still overruns by one.

The warning text is also off by one in its wording. With epochs `0..N` the vector has length `N + 1`, so `"The model fit only {max_epoch} epochs"` reports one more epoch than was actually fit.

## Reproducible example

```r
library(brulee)

set.seed(1)
torch::torch_manual_seed(1)
n <- 200
df <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n))
df$y <- df$x1 - 2 * df$x2 + rnorm(n)

fit <- brulee_mlp(y ~ ., df, epochs = 30, batch_size = 32)

# Stand in for a fit that early-stopped after 7 epochs, so `estimates` holds
# epochs 0-7 and the largest valid `epoch` is 7.
fit$estimates <- fit$estimates[1:8]

# Warns that the last epoch will be used, then errors anyway.
predict(fit, df, epoch = 10)
#> Warning: The model fit only 8 epochs; predictions cannot be made at epoch 10,
#>   so last epoch is used.
#> Error in model$estimates[[epoch + 1]] : subscript out of bounds

# `epoch` equal to `length(estimates)` slips past the guard entirely: no warning.
predict(fit, df, epoch = 8)
#> Error in model$estimates[[epoch + 1]] : subscript out of bounds

# `coef()` gets both cases right.
coef(fit, epoch = 10)
#> Warning: There were only 7 epochs fit. Setting `epochs` to 7.
```

## Why it matters

How many epochs a model actually fits depends on early stopping, which varies with platform, BLAS, and RNG. Code that passes a fixed `epoch` can therefore work on one machine and fail on another with an error that points at brulee internals rather than at the user's call.

This is what broke CI on macOS r-release in #137: an example used `epoch = 10` on a `brulee_mlp()` fit that reached 28 epochs locally but early-stopped sooner on the runner. Tests passed; only the example failed.

```
Error in model$estimates[[epoch + 1]] : subscript out of bounds
Calls: withAutoprint ... predict_brulee_mlp_bridge -> predict_function -> predict_brulee_mlp_raw
```

https://github.com/tidymodels/brulee/actions/runs/33635003768/job/100263553047

That example was changed to use a low epoch as a local workaround, which fixes the symptom but leaves the trap in place for users.

## Suggested fix

Make `last_epoch_note()` return the epoch to use and clamp to `length(estimates) - 1L`, then have each bridge assign its result:

```r
epoch <- last_epoch_note(epoch, length(model$estimates), call = call)
```

`brulee_coefs()` (`R/coef.R:10-21`) already does exactly this and can be the model for it, including the correct `- 1L`. Worth folding the bespoke clamp in `R/rln-predict.R:78-82` into the shared helper at the same time so the eight predict methods agree.

Affects every model with an `epoch` argument: `brulee_mlp()`, `brulee_linear_reg()`, `brulee_logistic_reg()`, `brulee_multinomial_reg()`, `brulee_resnet()`, `brulee_rln()`, `brulee_saint()`, and `brulee_auto_int()`.

A test that pins both cases (an epoch past the end, and an epoch exactly equal to `length(estimates)`) would keep it from regressing.

title: `brulee_resnet()` predicts all-`NA` when the trailing/last training batch has only 1 row
description:
`brulee_resnet()` returns all-`NA` predictions while reporting a finite training loss — with no error or warning.

**Cause:** when the training-set size isn't a multiple of `batch_size`, the trailing batch holds the remainder. If that remainder is a single row, batch-norm computes variance over 1 sample (`/(n - 1) = /0`), producing `NaN` in its `running_var` buffers.

**Why it's silent:** during training batch-norm uses per-batch statistics (`train()` mode), so the loss stays finite. `predict()` runs in `eval()` mode, which reads the `NaN` `running_var` — so every prediction becomes `NaN` (surfaced as `NA`).

**Scope:** any dataset size where the trailing batch is 1 row (e.g. 1001 rows with `batch_size = 100`); it is not specific to small data. It also happens on defaults — `mtcars` below hits it (32 rows → batch_size 4 → 29 training rows → a 1-row trailing batch). `brulee_mlp()` and `brulee_rln()` are unaffected (no batch-norm).

**Suggested fix:** drop a size-1 trailing batch (`drop_last`-style), or guard batch-norm against `n = 1`.

``` r
library(brulee)
library(recipes)
rec <- recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
set.seed(1)
fit <- brulee_resnet(rec, data = mtcars, hidden_units = 4, epochs = 5)
all(is.na(predict(fit, mtcars)$.pred)) 
#> [1] TRUE
all(is.finite(fit$loss))               
#> [1] TRUE
# the corrupted buffer:
any(is.nan(as.array(
  fit$estimates[[length(fit$estimates)]][["bn_out.running_var"]]
)))                                    
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: `predict.brulee_chronos()` requires the outcome column in `new_data`
description:
## Description

`predict.brulee_chronos()` forges `new_data` with `outcomes = TRUE` (R/chronos2-predict.R#L145), forcing the outcome column to be present at predict time. This breaks the tidymodels contract where `new_data` carries predictors only, so prediction through a workflow or `fit_resamples()` fails with `The required column "..y" is missing` — the root cause of tidymodels/tabular#10. Since `predict()` already forecasts from the fit-time context when `new_data = NULL` (R/chronos2-predict.R#L138), the covariate branch should do the same and treat `new_data` as covariates-only (`outcomes = FALSE`).

## Reprex

```r
library(brulee)

set.seed(1856)
train <- data.frame(y = cumsum(rnorm(200)), x = rnorm(200))
fit <- brulee_chronos(y ~ ., data = train, prediction_length = 14)

# At predict time you have covariates, not the outcome:
predict(fit, new_data = data.frame(x = rnorm(14)))
#> Error in `hardhat::forge()`:
#> ! The required column "y" is missing.

# It only succeeds if you supply the outcome it's meant to forecast:
predict(fit, new_data = data.frame(x = rnorm(14), y = rnorm(14)))
#> # A tibble: 14 × 2
#>      .pred .pred_quantile
```

title: brulee model does not use GPU with torch 0.16.0
description:
I'm having an issue where brulee models are not training on the GPU, despite the environment seemingly being set up correctly. The model training silently falls back to the CPU, while pure torch models do run successfully on the GPU.

Environment Details:

- brulee version: 0.6.0
- torch version: 0.16.0
- tidymodels version: 1.4.1

GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070
OS: Windows

Troubleshooting Steps:

- When fitting a brulee model, nvidia-smi shows 0% GPU utilization and the R process does not appear.
- Running torch::cuda_is_available() in the R console returns TRUE.
- Manually creating a tensor and moving it with x$cuda() succeeds.
- A pure torch training loop (with no brulee or tidymodels code) runs successfully on the GPU, with high utilization shown in nvidia-smi. 

This brulee code fails to use the GPU:

```r
library(tidymodels)
library(brulee)

# Fails to run on GPU
mlp_spec <- mlp(hidden_units = 500, epochs = 20000) %>%
  set_engine("brulee") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

mlp_wflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(recipe(Species ~ ., data = iris)) %>%
  add_model(mlp_spec)

fit(mlp_wflow, data = iris)
```

This code uses the GPU:
```r
library(torch)

model <- nn_sequential(
  nn_linear(4, 500), nn_relu(), nn_linear(500, 3)
)$to(device = "cuda")

x_train <- as_torch_tensor(as.matrix(iris[, 1:4]), device = "cuda")
y_train <- as_torch_tensor(as.integer(iris$Species), device = "cuda")

optimizer <- optim_adam(model$parameters, lr = 0.01)
loss_fn <- nn_cross_entropy_loss()

for (i in 1:20000) {
  optimizer$zero_grad()
  output <- model(x_train)
  loss <- loss_fn(output, y_train)
  loss$backward()
  optimizer$step()
}
```

title: Breaking changes - torch 0.11.0
description:
When predicting on new data with the updated torch version 0.11.0 I get an error `!self$..refer_to_state_dict.. : invalid argument type`. I believe it is linked to the breaking change mentioned below.

## Breaking changes - torch 0.11.0

* [load_state_dict()](https://torch.mlverse.org/docs/reference/load_state_dict.html) for optimizers now default to cloning the tensors in the state dict, so they don’t keep references to objects in the dict. ([#1041](https://github.com/mlverse/torch/issues/1041))

## Reproducible example

```r
install.packages("torch") # Version 0.11.0
torch::install_torch(reinstall = TRUE)
library(brulee)
library(recipes)
library(yardstick)

data(bivariate, package = "modeldata")
set.seed(20)
nn_log_biv <- brulee_mlp(Class ~ log(A) + log(B), data = bivariate_train, 
                         epochs = 150, hidden_units = 3)

# We use the tidymodels semantics to always return a tibble when predicting
predict(nn_log_biv, bivariate_test, type = "prob") %>% 
  bind_cols(bivariate_test) %>% 
  roc_auc(Class, .pred_One)

# Error in !self$..refer_to_state_dict.. : invalid argument type
```

title: learning rate schemes
description:
From @dfalbel...

We might want to implement a learning rate decay technique otherwise it's too hard to tune the learning rate correctly.

Maybe something like what sklearn does:

- ‘invscaling’ gradually decreases the learning rate at each time step ‘t’ using an inverse scaling exponent of ‘power_t’. effective_learning_rate = learning_rate_init / pow(t, power_t)

- ‘adaptive’ keeps the learning rate constant to ‘learning_rate_init’ as long as training loss keeps decreasing. Each time two consecutive epochs fail to decrease training loss by at least tol, or fail to increase validation score by at least tol if ‘early_stopping’ is on, the current learning rate is divided by 5.
